notes: Reasoning Ability part of BATCH_005: 200 original questions (60 Basic, 80 Intermediate, 60 Advanced) built by tools/batch_005/reasoning.py. New puzzle structures and noun sets. Puzzles are brute-forced for a unique arrangement; syllogisms are checked over every Venn-region model; inequalities over all integer assignments; data sufficiency by enumerating models for each statement subset; blood relations, directions, coding (inferred rules checked against alternative simple rules), series, alphabet, number operations, ranking and input-output are recomputed in code. Verbal-reasoning items are hand-written and were re-answered blind by a separate solver. All questions await human review.

stimuli.title: Seven persons in a row, with favourite vegetables
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Bhavik, Dhwani, Garv, Ipsita, Mayank, Sarthak and Tamanna sit in a straight row, all facing north. Each of them likes a different vegetable among Beans, Brinjal, Cabbage, Carrot, Okra, Peas and Spinach. (Facing north, a person's right is towards the east end of the row.)

- Ipsita sits exactly in the middle of the row.
- Dhwani sits second to the right of Ipsita.
- Mayank sits immediately to the right of Dhwani.
- The person who likes Carrot sits immediately to the left of Ipsita, and that person is Bhavik.
- Garv sits at one of the extreme ends of the row.
- Sarthak is not an immediate neighbour of Garv.
- The person who likes Okra sits immediately to the right of Garv.
- Ipsita likes Spinach, and Mayank likes Brinjal.
- The person who likes Beans sits immediately to the left of the person who likes Cabbage.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Number the seats 1 to 7 from the left. Ipsita = 4, Dhwani = 6, Mayank = 7.
Step 2: The Carrot-lover sits at seat 3 and is Bhavik.
Step 3: Garv is at an end; seat 7 is Mayank's, so Garv = 1. Seats 2 and 5 remain for Sarthak and Tamanna; Sarthak cannot sit next to Garv, so Sarthak = 5 and Tamanna = 2.
Step 4: Okra is immediately right of Garv: Tamanna. Ipsita Spinach, Mayank Brinjal.
Step 5: Beans, Cabbage and Peas remain for Garv (1), Sarthak (5) and Dhwani (6). Beans is immediately left of Cabbage, so Sarthak Beans, Dhwani Cabbage and Garv Peas.

| Seat | Person | Vegetable |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Garv | Peas |
| 2 | Tamanna | Okra |
| 3 | Bhavik | Carrot |
| 4 | Ipsita | Spinach |
| 5 | Sarthak | Beans |
| 6 | Dhwani | Cabbage |
| 7 | Mayank | Brinjal |

stimuli.title: Six persons in two short facing rows
stimuli.content:
Six persons Kuhu, Lakshay, Nivedita, Pranit, Sanya and Vishal sit in two parallel rows of three seats each. The persons in Row 1 face south and the persons in Row 2 face north, so each person faces exactly one person of the other row. (Facing south, the right is towards the west; facing north, the right is towards the east.)

- Pranit sits in the middle seat of the row that faces south.
- Lakshay faces Pranit.
- Sanya sits immediately to the left of Pranit.
- Vishal sits immediately to the left of Lakshay.
- Nivedita faces Sanya.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 1 to 3 from west to east in both rows.
Step 1: Pranit = Row 1 seat 2; Lakshay faces him: Row 2 seat 2.
Step 2: Pranit faces south, so his left is east: Sanya = Row 1 seat 3. Lakshay faces north, so his left is west: Vishal = Row 2 seat 1.
Step 3: Nivedita faces Sanya: Row 2 seat 3. Kuhu takes the last seat, Row 1 seat 1.

| Seat | Row 1 (facing south) | Row 2 (facing north) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Kuhu | Vishal |
| 2 | Pranit | Lakshay |
| 3 | Sanya | Nivedita |

stimuli.title: Eight persons on ten facing seats, one vacant seat per row
stimuli.content:
Ten seats are arranged in two parallel rows of five, numbered 1 to 5 from west to east in each row. The persons in Row 1 face south and those in Row 2 face north, so seat k of Row 1 faces seat k of Row 2. Eight persons Bhagya, Darshit, Hritik, Jhilmil, Kalindi, Nirmay, Rudra and Tejasvi sit on eight of the seats, and exactly one seat in each row is vacant. (Facing south, the right is west; facing north, the right is east. Vacant seats are counted as seats.)

- Kalindi faces south and sits in the middle seat of her row; Nirmay faces Kalindi.
- Bhagya sits immediately to the left of Kalindi, and the seat facing Bhagya is vacant.
- Darshit sits second to the left of the vacant seat in his row.
- Hritik sits third to the right of Bhagya.
- Rudra sits at an extreme end of a row.
- Jhilmil faces north and faces Rudra.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Kalindi = Row 1 seat 3 (facing south, so her right is west and her left east); Nirmay = Row 2 seat 3.
Step 2: Bhagya is immediately to Kalindi's left: Row 1 seat 4, and the seat facing him, Row 2 seat 4, is vacant. Hritik is third to Bhagya's right (west): Row 1 seat 1.
Step 3: Jhilmil is in Row 2 and faces Rudra, so Rudra is in Row 1, at an end: seat 5 (seat 1 is Hritik's). Jhilmil = Row 2 seat 5.
Step 4: Row 2 already has its vacant seat (4), so Tejasvi and Darshit fill Row 2 seats 1 and 2 and Row 1 seat 2 is vacant. Darshit is second to the left of his row's vacant seat: in Row 2 (facing north, left = west) that is seat 2. (In Row 1 the seat second to the left of vacant seat 2 would be Bhagya's seat 4.) So Darshit = Row 2 seat 2 and Tejasvi = Row 2 seat 1.

| Seat | Row 1 (facing south) | Row 2 (facing north) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hritik | Tejasvi |
| 2 | vacant | Darshit |
| 3 | Kalindi | Nirmay |
| 4 | Bhagya | vacant |
| 5 | Rudra | Jhilmil |

stimuli.title: Eight persons around a round table
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Aadhya, Bhrigu, Cauvery, Jagrav, Lohith, Mahika, Ranveer and Sukriti sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. (Facing the centre, a person's right is anticlockwise.)

- Mahika sits opposite Aadhya.
- Lohith sits immediately to the right of Aadhya, and Sukriti sits second to the right of Aadhya.
- Bhrigu sits immediately to the left of Mahika.
- Cauvery sits second to the left of Aadhya.
- Jagrav is not an immediate neighbour of Aadhya.
stimuli.solution:
Put Aadhya at seat 0 and number the seats anticlockwise. Mahika = 4. Lohith = 1, Sukriti = 2. Bhrigu (immediately left of Mahika) = 3. Cauvery (second to Aadhya's left) = 6. Seats 5 and 7 remain for Jagrav and Ranveer; seat 7 is next to Aadhya, so Jagrav = 5 and Ranveer = 7.

Anticlockwise from Aadhya (each person's right is the next seat anticlockwise): Aadhya, Lohith, Sukriti, Bhrigu, Mahika, Jagrav, Cauvery, Ranveer

stimuli.title: Ten persons around a round table
stimuli.content:
Ten persons Agastya, Binal, Chanchal, Dhairya, Ipshita, Kanishk, Nandan, Pavani, Shaurya and Vanshika sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. (Facing the centre, a person's right is anticlockwise.)

- Nandan sits opposite Agastya.
- Dhairya sits second to the right of Agastya.
- Only one person sits between Dhairya and Binal when counted to the right of Dhairya, and that person is Shaurya.
- Chanchal sits third to the right of Nandan.
- Vanshika is an immediate neighbour of Nandan.
- Kanishk sits immediately to the left of Chanchal.
- Ipshita sits immediately to the left of Agastya.
stimuli.solution:
Put Agastya at seat 0 and number the seats 0 to 9 anticlockwise. Nandan = 5. Dhairya = 2, Shaurya = 3, Binal = 4. Chanchal = 5 + 3 = 8 and Kanishk = 7. Nandan's neighbours are seats 4 (Binal) and 6, so Vanshika = 6. Ipshita = 9, and Pavani takes the last seat, 1.

Anticlockwise from Agastya: Agastya, Pavani, Dhairya, Shaurya, Binal, Nandan, Vanshika, Kanishk, Chanchal, Ipshita

stimuli.title: Square table: corners facing out, sides facing in
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Avni, Chirantan, Gulabo, Jaiveer, Lavleen, Prithvi, Tanuja and Yashpal sit around a square table. Four of them sit at the four corners and face outside (away from the centre); the other four sit at the middle of the four sides and face the centre. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise; facing outside, the right is clockwise.)

- Avni sits at a corner of the table.
- Prithvi sits immediately to the left of Avni, and Yashpal sits opposite Avni.
- Gulabo sits second to the right of Prithvi.
- Tanuja sits immediately to the left of Gulabo.
- Chirantan sits immediately to the left of Yashpal.
- Jaiveer sits at the middle of a side.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 0 to 7 anticlockwise with Avni's corner as 0; corners are the even seats.
Step 1: Avni faces outside, so her left is anticlockwise: Prithvi = 1. Yashpal = 4.
Step 2: Prithvi faces the centre, so his right is anticlockwise: Gulabo = 3. Gulabo faces the centre, so her left is clockwise: Tanuja = 2.
Step 3: Yashpal (corner, facing outside) has his left anticlockwise: Chirantan = 5.
Step 4: Seats 6 (corner) and 7 (side) remain; Jaiveer sits at a side: Jaiveer = 7, Lavleen = 6.

Anticlockwise from Avni: Avni (corner, facing outside), Prithvi (side, facing the centre), Tanuja (corner, facing outside), Gulabo (side, facing the centre), Yashpal (corner, facing outside), Chirantan (side, facing the centre), Lavleen (corner, facing outside), Jaiveer (side, facing the centre)

stimuli.title: Seven persons, one empty chair, facing in or out
stimuli.content:
Eight chairs are placed around a circular table, equally spaced. Seven persons Abhimanyu, Chitrangada, Devraj, Gauhar, Malti, Parikshit and Satyam sit on seven of them; one chair is vacant. Some of the persons face the centre and the others face outside. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise; facing outside, the right is clockwise.) Positions such as 'second to the right' count chairs, including the vacant one.

- Abhimanyu faces the centre, and the vacant chair is second to his right.
- Satyam sits opposite Abhimanyu.
- Devraj sits between the vacant chair and Satyam, next to both.
- Gauhar sits immediately to the left of Satyam, and Parikshit sits immediately to the right of Gauhar.
- Devraj sits second to the left of Malti.
- Parikshit faces the same direction as Abhimanyu, and Chitrangada faces the direction opposite to Parikshit's.
- Exactly three persons face outside.
stimuli.solution:
Put Abhimanyu at chair 0 and number the chairs anticlockwise.
Step 1: Abhimanyu faces the centre, so chair 2 is vacant. Satyam = 4, and Devraj (between the vacant chair and Satyam) = 3.
Step 2: If Satyam faced the centre, his left (clockwise) would be chair 3, Devraj's; so Satyam faces outside and Gauhar = 5. If Gauhar faced outside, his right would be chair 4 (Satyam); so Gauhar faces the centre and Parikshit = 6. Chairs 1 and 7 remain.
Step 3: Devraj is second to Malti's left. From chair 1 facing outside (left = anticlockwise) that is chair 3 — it fits; from chair 7 either way it is chair 1 or chair 5 — neither is Devraj's. So Malti = 1 and faces outside, and Chitrangada = 7.
Step 4: Parikshit faces the centre like Abhimanyu, so Chitrangada faces outside. Outside: Satyam, Malti, Chitrangada — three — so Devraj faces the centre.

Anticlockwise from Abhimanyu: Abhimanyu (facing the centre), Malti (facing outside), vacant chair, Devraj (facing the centre), Satyam (facing outside), Gauhar (facing the centre), Parikshit (facing the centre), Chitrangada (facing outside)

stimuli.title: Six cricketers around a table, with their runs
stimuli.content:
Six persons Hrishikesh, Inder, Jasmit, Kaveri, Lalitesh and Nayantara sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. In a match each of them scored a different number of runs among 12, 18, 25, 31, 40 and 47. (Facing the centre, a person's right is anticlockwise.)

- The person who scored 47 runs sits opposite the person who scored 12 runs.
- Inder scored 31 runs and sits immediately to the left of Kaveri, who scored the fewest runs.
- Hrishikesh sits opposite Inder.
- The runs of Hrishikesh's two immediate neighbours add up to 87.
- Jasmit scored more runs than Nayantara, and Lalitesh scored fewer runs than Hrishikesh.
stimuli.solution:
Put Inder at seat 0 and number the seats anticlockwise.
Step 1: Inder is immediately to Kaveri's left (clockwise of her), so Kaveri = 1, with 12 runs; Inder has 31. Hrishikesh = 3.
Step 2: The 47-scorer sits opposite Kaveri: seat 4.
Step 3: Hrishikesh's neighbours are seats 2 and 4. Seat 4 has 47, so seat 2 has 87 − 47 = 40.
Step 4: Jasmit, Lalitesh and Nayantara take seats 2, 4 and 5. Lalitesh scored fewer than Hrishikesh, and Hrishikesh cannot have 40 or 47 (they are at seats 2 and 4), so Lalitesh cannot hold 40 or 47 either: Lalitesh = seat 5. Jasmit > Nayantara gives Jasmit 47 (seat 4) and Nayantara 40 (seat 2). Hrishikesh and Lalitesh share 18 and 25; Lalitesh has fewer: Lalitesh 18, Hrishikesh 25.

| Seat | Person | Runs |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Inder | 31 |
| 1 | Kaveri | 12 |
| 2 | Nayantara | 40 |
| 3 | Hrishikesh | 25 |
| 4 | Jasmit | 47 |
| 5 | Lalitesh | 18 |

stimuli.title: Six floors and six favourite sweets
stimuli.content:
Six persons Ayush, Charulata, Dakshesh, Hemangi, Kiranmayi and Sohil live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor. Floor 1 is the lowermost and floor 6 the topmost. Each of them likes a different sweet among Barfi, Halwa, Jalebi, Laddoo, Peda and Rasgulla.

- Ayush lives on floor 3 and likes Halwa.
- Only one person lives between Ayush and Dakshesh, and Dakshesh lives above Ayush.
- Charulata lives immediately above Dakshesh and likes Laddoo.
- Kiranmayi lives immediately above Ayush.
- Hemangi lives on an even-numbered floor.
- The person who likes Peda lives on the lowermost floor, and the person who likes Jalebi lives immediately below Ayush.
- The person who likes Rasgulla lives immediately above the person who likes Barfi.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Ayush = 3, Dakshesh = 5, Charulata = 6, Kiranmayi = 4.
Step 2: Floors 1 and 2 remain; Hemangi is on an even floor: Hemangi = 2, Sohil = 1.
Step 3: Peda is on floor 1 (Sohil); Jalebi on floor 2 (Hemangi). Barfi and Rasgulla remain for floors 4 and 5; Rasgulla is above Barfi: Kiranmayi Barfi, Dakshesh Rasgulla.

| Floor | Person | Sweet |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Charulata | Laddoo |
| 5 | Dakshesh | Rasgulla |
| 4 | Kiranmayi | Barfi |
| 3 | Ayush | Halwa |
| 2 | Hemangi | Jalebi |
| 1 | Sohil | Peda |

stimuli.title: Seven floors and seven monthly rents
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Anvay, Brijesh, Dhruvika, Gunjita, Jasraj, Moksha and Neelesh live on the seven floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 7 the topmost). Each pays a different monthly rent among ₹8,000, ₹9,000, ₹11,000, ₹12,000, ₹14,000, ₹15,000 and ₹17,000.

- Moksha lives on floor 4 and pays ₹14,000.
- The person who pays the highest rent lives two floors below Moksha.
- Jasraj lives immediately above Moksha and pays the lowest rent.
- Anvay lives immediately below Moksha, and his rent is ₹1,000 more than Jasraj's.
- Dhruvika lives on the topmost floor, and the rents of Dhruvika and Gunjita add up to ₹23,000.
- Brijesh pays ₹1,000 more than Moksha, and Gunjita lives below Brijesh.
- Gunjita pays more than Dhruvika.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Moksha = 4 (₹14,000). Jasraj = 5 (₹8,000, the lowest). Anvay = 3 (₹9,000). The ₹17,000 payer is on floor 2. Dhruvika = 7.
Step 2: Brijesh pays ₹15,000, so he is not on floor 2. Floors 1, 2 and 6 remain for Brijesh, Gunjita and Neelesh; Gunjita lives below Brijesh, so Brijesh cannot be on floor 1 — Brijesh = 6.
Step 3: Rents left: ₹11,000, ₹12,000 and ₹17,000 for Dhruvika, Gunjita and Neelesh. Dhruvika + Gunjita = ₹23,000 = 11 + 12, so Neelesh pays ₹17,000 and lives on floor 2; Gunjita = 1. Gunjita pays more than Dhruvika: Gunjita ₹12,000, Dhruvika ₹11,000.

| Floor | Person | Rent |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | Dhruvika | ₹11,000 |
| 6 | Brijesh | ₹15,000 |
| 5 | Jasraj | ₹8,000 |
| 4 | Moksha | ₹14,000 |
| 3 | Anvay | ₹9,000 |
| 2 | Neelesh | ₹17,000 |
| 1 | Gunjita | ₹12,000 |

stimuli.title: Nine floors numbered from the top, two vacant
stimuli.content:
A building has nine floors. The floors are numbered from the top: floor 1 is the topmost floor and floor 9 the lowermost. Seven persons Amarjeet, Bhuvanesh, Chinmayee, Durgesh, Pankti, Ritwik and Shalaka live in it, one person per floor, so two floors are vacant. Each person has a different profession among Actor, Baker, Coach, Dentist, Jeweller, Nurse and Plumber.

- Durgesh lives on floor 5 and is a Plumber.
- The Baker lives immediately above Durgesh, and the floor immediately below Durgesh is vacant.
- Bhuvanesh lives on the lowermost floor, and Chinmayee lives immediately above him.
- Pankti is a Dentist and lives immediately above Chinmayee.
- Amarjeet lives three floors above Pankti.
- Exactly one floor lies between Ritwik and Shalaka, and Ritwik lives above Shalaka.
- The Nurse lives immediately above the Baker.
- Ritwik is neither the Actor nor the Jeweller, and the Jeweller lives below the Actor.
stimuli.solution:
Remember: a smaller floor number is higher up.
Step 1: Durgesh = 5 (Plumber); floor 6 is vacant; the Baker is on floor 4.
Step 2: Bhuvanesh = 9, Chinmayee = 8, Pankti = 7 (Dentist). Amarjeet = 7 − 3 = 4, so Amarjeet is the Baker.
Step 3: Floors 1, 2 and 3 remain for Ritwik and Shalaka, with one floor between them and Ritwik higher: Ritwik = 1, Shalaka = 3, floor 2 vacant.
Step 4: The Nurse is immediately above the Baker (floor 4): Shalaka. Actor, Coach and Jeweller remain for Ritwik, Chinmayee and Bhuvanesh; Ritwik is the Coach. The Jeweller is below the Actor: Bhuvanesh (9) Jeweller, Chinmayee (8) Actor.

| Floor (from top) | Person | Profession |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ritwik | Coach |
| 2 | vacant | — |
| 3 | Shalaka | Nurse |
| 4 | Amarjeet | Baker |
| 5 | Durgesh | Plumber |
| 6 | vacant | — |
| 7 | Pankti | Dentist |
| 8 | Chinmayee | Actor |
| 9 | Bhuvanesh | Jeweller |

stimuli.title: Seven boxes in one stack
stimuli.content:
Seven boxes B, E, G, J, N, S and W are kept one above another in a single stack. Position 1 is the bottom and position 7 the top.

- Box W is kept exactly in the middle of the stack.
- Only two boxes are kept between box W and box G, and box G is above box W.
- Box B is kept immediately above box W.
- Box J is kept at the bottom of the stack.
- Box E is kept immediately above box S.
stimuli.solution:
W = 4, G = 7, B = 5, J = 1. Positions 2, 3 and 6 remain for E, N and S. E is immediately above S, so they take 2 and 3 (S = 2, E = 3), and N = 6.

Bottom to top: J, S, E, W, B, N, G

stimuli.title: Ten boxes in two side-by-side stacks
stimuli.content:
Ten boxes B, D, F, H, K, M, P, R, T and W are kept in two stacks, Left and Right, standing side by side, with five boxes in each stack. Level 1 is the bottom of a stack and level 5 its top. A box is 'directly to the right' of another when it is at the same level of the Right stack.

- Box T is at level 3 of the left stack, and box F is directly to the right of box T (at the same level of the other stack).
- Box P is kept immediately above box F, and box H is at the top of the stack that contains box P.
- Box B is at the same level as box P, in the other stack.
- Box K is at the bottom of the stack that does not contain box H.
- Boxes B and D are in the same stack, and as many boxes are kept above box B as below box D.
- Box W is kept immediately above box M, and box R is not in the stack that contains box W.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: T = Left 3, F = Right 3, P = Right 4, H = Right 5. B is at level 4 of the Left stack.
Step 2: K is at the bottom of the stack without H: Left 1.
Step 3: D is in B's stack (Left). One box is above B (level 5), so one box is below D: D = Left 2.
Step 4: Left 5, Right 1 and Right 2 remain for M, R and W. W is immediately above M, so they take Right 1 and Right 2 (M = Right 1, W = Right 2); R is in the other stack: Left 5.

| Level | Left stack | Right stack |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | R | H |
| 4 | B | P |
| 3 | T | F |
| 2 | D | W |
| 1 | K | M |

stimuli.title: Eight boxes in eight colours
stimuli.content:
Eight boxes C, E, H, L, O, S, V and Y are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom and 8 the top). Each box is of a different colour among Brown, Cream, Golden, Grey, Navy, Olive, Peach and Silver.

- Box C is kept fourth from the bottom.
- Only two boxes are kept between box C and the Cream box, and the Cream box is above C.
- Box L is kept immediately above box V, which is not Grey.
- Box S is at the bottom and is Navy.
- The Olive box is kept immediately above the Golden box, and box Y is Golden.
- Box O is kept immediately above box C, and box E is kept immediately below box V.
- Box L is Brown, box H is Peach, and box O is not Grey.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: C = 4; the Cream box is at 7; O = 5; S = 1 (Navy).
Step 2: L is immediately above V and E immediately below V, so E, V, L occupy three consecutive positions among the free ones (2, 3, 6, 7, 8): only 6, 7, 8 work. E = 6, V = 7 (Cream), L = 8 (Brown).
Step 3: H and Y take 2 and 3. The Olive box is immediately above the Golden box Y. If Y were at 2, position 3 would be Olive, but H at 3 is Peach; so Y = 3 and H = 2, and C (position 4) is Olive.
Step 4: Grey and Silver remain for O and E; O is not Grey, so O is Silver and E is Grey.

| Position | Box | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | L | Brown |
| 7 | V | Cream |
| 6 | E | Grey |
| 5 | O | Silver |
| 4 | C | Olive |
| 3 | Y | Golden |
| 2 | H | Peach |
| 1 | S | Navy |

stimuli.title: Six meetings in six months, with cities
stimuli.content:
Six persons Aruna, Bhaskar, Gauravi, Jitesh, Madhulika and Sameer each attend one meeting in the same non-leap year. The meetings are held in six different months — February, March, May, July, August and November — and in six different cities among Ajmer, Bareilly, Hubli, Jorhat, Nashik and Rourkela. 'Between' and 'next' refer to the order of these six meetings.

- Gauravi's meeting is in a month that has 31 days, and it is held in Jorhat.
- Exactly two of the meetings are held between Gauravi's and Jitesh's, and Jitesh's is earlier.
- Madhulika's meeting is the last of the six.
- Bhaskar's meeting is the next one after Gauravi's, and it is held in Rourkela.
- Aruna's meeting is earlier than Sameer's.
- The Hubli meeting is in the shortest of the six months, and the Ajmer meeting is the one just before Gauravi's.
- The Nashik meeting is in a month that has 31 days.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Gauravi's month has 31 days: March, May, July or August. Jitesh is three meetings earlier, so Gauravi is in July (Jitesh February) or August (Jitesh March).
Step 2: Bhaskar is the next meeting after Gauravi's. If Gauravi were in August, Bhaskar would be in November, which is Madhulika's. So Gauravi = July, Jitesh = February, Bhaskar = August.
Step 3: Aruna and Sameer take March and May; Aruna is earlier: Aruna March, Sameer May.
Step 4: Hubli is in February (Jitesh); Ajmer is just before July: May (Sameer). Bareilly and Nashik remain for March and November; Nashik is in a 31-day month: Aruna Nashik, Madhulika Bareilly.

| Month | Person | City |
|---|---|---|
| February | Jitesh | Hubli |
| March | Aruna | Nashik |
| May | Sameer | Ajmer |
| July | Gauravi | Jorhat |
| August | Bhaskar | Rourkela |
| November | Madhulika | Bareilly |

stimuli.title: Appointments on the Tuesdays and Fridays of October 2026
stimuli.content:
A bank's loan officer meets customers only on Tuesdays and Fridays. Eight customers Chandrima, Dheeraj, Farhana, Jugnu, Kshitij, Mahua, Prachi and Rishabh each have one appointment with her in October 2026, on eight different dates; one of the possible dates has no appointment. 1 October 2026 is a Thursday.

- Chandrima's appointment is on the third Friday of the month.
- Only two persons have appointments between Chandrima's and Dheeraj's, and Dheeraj's is later.
- Mahua's appointment is on the last of the nine possible dates.
- No appointment is fixed on the second Friday of the month.
- Farhana's appointment is on the possible date immediately before Chandrima's.
- Kshitij's appointment is on the first Tuesday, and Prachi's is earlier than Kshitij's.
- Jugnu's appointment is on a Tuesday.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: 1 October is a Thursday, so the Fridays are 2, 9, 16, 23, 30 and the Tuesdays 6, 13, 20, 27: nine possible dates.
Step 2: Chandrima = 16 (third Friday); the 9th has no appointment; Mahua = 30; Farhana = 13 (the possible date just before the 16th). Kshitij = 6 (first Tuesday), so Prachi = 2.
Step 3: The 20th, 23rd and 27th remain for Dheeraj, Jugnu and Rishabh. Two persons sit between Chandrima and Dheeraj, so Dheeraj = 27. Jugnu is on a Tuesday: 20; Rishabh = 23.

| Date | Day | Customer |
|---|---|---|
| 2 Oct | Friday | Prachi |
| 6 Oct | Tuesday | Kshitij |
| 9 Oct | Friday | — |
| 13 Oct | Tuesday | Farhana |
| 16 Oct | Friday | Chandrima |
| 20 Oct | Tuesday | Jugnu |
| 23 Oct | Friday | Rishabh |
| 27 Oct | Tuesday | Dheeraj |

stimuli.title: Five calculus-style inequality symbols
stimuli.content:
In the questions of this set, the symbols ∂, ∇, ∫, ∑ and ∏ are used with these meanings:
'A ∂ B' means 'A is greater than B'; 'A ∇ B' means 'A is smaller than B'; 'A ∫ B' means 'A is equal to B'; 'A ∑ B' means 'A is either greater than or equal to B'; 'A ∏ B' means 'A is either smaller than or equal to B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Decode: ∂ means >, ∇ means <, ∫ means =, ∑ means ≥ and ∏ means ≤. Rewrite every statement with the ordinary signs, join them into one chain, and test each conclusion along the chain.

stimuli.title: Three coded sentences about a river
stimuli.content:
In a certain code language:
'river flows fast' is written as 'mo ki ra',
'fast boats sail' is written as 'ki pu zo', and
'boats cross river' is written as 'zo ra te'.
(The codes of the words in a sentence may be in any order.)
stimuli.solution: Each shared word takes the code its two sentences share: river = ra (sentences 1 and 3), fast = ki (1 and 2), boats = zo (2 and 3). The leftover code in each sentence belongs to its only unshared word: flows = mo, sail = pu, cross = te.

stimuli.content:
Each letter is coded as shown below, subject to the conditions that follow.

| Letter | A | B | C | D | E | H | K | M | N | O | R | S | T | U |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C | o | d | e |
| 4 |
| % |
| 7 |
| @ |
| 9 |
| # |
| 2 |
| $ |
| 5 |
| 8 |
| & |

Conditions:
(i) If the first letter is a vowel and the last letter is a consonant, the codes of the first and the last letters are interchanged.
(ii) If both the first and the last letters are vowels, both are coded as the code of the second letter.
(iii) If the first letter is a consonant and the last letter is a vowel, the last letter is coded as ★.
If no condition applies, every letter is coded as in the table.
stimuli.solution: Check the first and last letters of the word, apply at most one condition, and code the remaining letters from the table.

stimuli.title: Four coded sentences about plants
stimuli.content:
In a certain code language:
'save water daily' is written as 'ka lo mi',
'water the plants daily' is written as 'mi ne lo su',
'plants need sunlight' is written as 'su ra tu', and
'need to save' is written as 'ra ka vo'.
(The codes of the words in a sentence may be in any order.)
stimuli.solution: plants = su (sentences 2 and 3); need = ra (3 and 4); save = ka (1 and 4). Then sunlight = tu and to = vo. 'water' and 'daily' always appear together, so they share 'lo' and 'mi' in some order; the remaining code of sentence 2, ne, is 'the'.

stimuli.title: Six three-digit numbers
stimuli.content:
Study the following six three-digit numbers and answer the questions.

517   284   936   461   708   359
stimuli.solution: Read each operation carefully and apply it to every number.

stimuli.title: Three rows of numbers with operation rules
stimuli.content:
Each row below has three numbers. Work from left to right: apply the rule that fits the first two numbers, then apply the rule that fits that result and the third number. The final value is the row's result.

(i) If an odd number is followed by an even number, they are added.
(ii) If an even number is followed by an odd number, the odd number is subtracted from the even number.
(iii) If an odd number is followed by an odd number, they are multiplied.
(iv) If an even number is followed by an even number, the first is divided by the second.

Row 1: 15   8   3
Row 2: 36   4   7
Row 3: 28   5   6
stimuli.solution:
Row 1: 15 (odd), 8 (even) → 23; 23, 3 (both odd) → 69.
Row 2: 36, 4 (both even) → 9; 9, 7 (both odd) → 63.
Row 3: 28 (even), 5 (odd) → 23; 23 (odd), 6 (even) → 29.

stimuli.title: Machine: smallest number to the right end
stimuli.content:
A number arrangement machine rearranges a line of numbers step by step. In each step it takes the smallest number among those not yet arranged and places it at the right end, immediately to the left of the numbers already arranged there (in Step I, at the extreme right). The other numbers keep their order. The machine stops when all the numbers are arranged.

Input: 48 13 76 54 29 37 91

stimuli.title: Machine: words rotated and moved to the right
stimuli.content:
A word arrangement machine rearranges a line of words step by step. In each step it takes, among the words not yet arranged, the word that comes first in alphabetical order, moves its first letter to the end of the word (for example, 'pear' becomes 'earp'), and places the new word at the right end, immediately to the left of the words already arranged there. The other words keep their order. The machine stops when every word has been arranged.

Input: plum grape kiwi apple mango lime
stimuli.solution:
Alphabetical order of the input words: apple, grape, kiwi, lime, mango, plum.

Step I: plum grape kiwi mango lime pplea
Step II: plum kiwi mango lime rapeg pplea
Step III: plum mango lime iwik rapeg pplea
Step IV: plum mango imel iwik rapeg pplea
Step V: plum angom imel iwik rapeg pplea
Step VI: lump angom imel iwik rapeg pplea

stimuli.title: Machine: digit products and reversed words
stimuli.content:
A word and number arrangement machine rearranges a line step by step. In each step it makes two moves: (1) among the numbers not yet arranged, it takes the one whose two digits have the smallest product, replaces it by the sum of its digits and places the result at the left end, immediately to the right of the results already placed there; (2) among the words not yet arranged, it takes the one that comes last in alphabetical order, writes it backwards and places it at the right end, immediately to the left of the words already placed there. All other elements keep their order. The machine stops when every element has been arranged.

Input: comet 47 orbit 82 nova 36 lunar 91 star 55
stimuli.solution:
Digit products: 47 → 28, 82 → 16, 36 → 18, 91 → 9, 55 → 25, so the numbers are taken in the order 91, 82, 36, 55, 47 and become 10, 10, 9, 10, 11. Words from last to first alphabetically: star, orbit, nova, lunar, comet.

Step I: 10 comet 47 orbit 82 nova 36 lunar 55 rats
Step II: 10 10 comet 47 nova 36 lunar 55 tibro rats
Step III: 10 10 9 comet 47 lunar 55 avon tibro rats
Step IV: 10 10 9 10 comet 47 ranul avon tibro rats
Step V: 10 10 9 10 11 temoc ranul avon tibro rats

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Some persons sit in a straight row, all facing north. The number of persons is not given.
- Ketan sits ninth from the left end.
- Lipika sits to the right of Ketan, and exactly as many persons sit between Ketan and Lipika as sit to the left of Ketan.
- Mohini sits fourth to the right of Lipika and is seventh from the right end.

How many persons sit in the row?

solution.concept: Turning a 'between' count into a position
solution.explanation: Eight persons sit to the left of Ketan (9th), so eight sit between Ketan and Lipika: Lipika is 9 + 8 + 1 = 18th. Mohini is 18 + 4 = 22nd from the left and 7th from the right, so the row has 22 + 7 − 1 = 28 persons.
steps: Left of Ketan: 8 ⇒ 8 persons between Ketan and Lipika
Lipika = 9 + 9 = 18th
Mohini = 22nd
solution.why_others_wrong: 27 places Lipika 17th (eight seats instead of eight persons between); 29 forgets to subtract Mohini once; 26 subtracts her twice.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Seven persons Anahita, Bodhan, Devyani, Eknoor, Gurdeep, Haimanti and Yug sit in a straight row. Some of them face north and the others face south. (Facing north, the right is east; facing south, the right is west.)
- Devyani sits in the middle seat and faces south.
- Yug sits immediately to the right of Devyani, and Bodhan sits immediately to her left.
- Haimanti sits third to the right of Yug.
- Bodhan faces the same direction as Yug.
- Anahita sits immediately to the left of Yug, and Gurdeep sits second to the left of Yug.
- Eknoor faces south, and Anahita faces the direction opposite to Yug's.
- Exactly three persons face south.

Who sits second to the right of Eknoor?

solution.concept: Fix each person's facing before reading 'right'
solution.explanation: Number the seats 1 to 7 from the west. Devyani = 4 facing south (right = west), so Yug = 3 and Bodhan = 5. Haimanti is third to Yug's right: if Yug faced south that would be seat 0, so Yug faces north and Haimanti = 6; Bodhan also faces north. Anahita (immediately left of Yug) = 2 and Gurdeep = 1, so Eknoor = 7. Eknoor, Devyani and Anahita (opposite to Yug) face south — already three — so Gurdeep and Haimanti face north. Eknoor faces south, so his right is west: seat 6 (Haimanti), then seat 5 (Bodhan).
steps: Devyani 4 (S) ⇒ Yug 3, Bodhan 5
Haimanti = Yug + 3 needs Yug facing north ⇒ Haimanti 6
Anahita 2, Gurdeep 1, Eknoor 7
South: Devyani, Anahita, Eknoor (three) ⇒ others north
Eknoor (7) faces south ⇒ second to his right = seat 5 = Bodhan
solution.why_others_wrong: Haimanti is immediately to Eknoor's right; Devyani is third to his right; Yug is fourth.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Eight persons Raunak, Shivangi, Tarak, Urmi, Vatsal, Waseem, Xenia and Zubair sit in a straight row, all facing north.
- Raunak sits fourth from the left end.
- Only two persons sit to the right of Shivangi.
- Xenia sits exactly midway between Raunak and Shivangi.
- Vatsal sits second to the right of Shivangi, and Waseem is an immediate neighbour of Vatsal.
- Zubair is an immediate neighbour of Raunak.
- Tarak is not an immediate neighbour of Zubair.

If Zubair and Vatsal interchange their seats, how many persons will then sit between Zubair and Xenia?

solution.concept: Fix the row, then apply the interchange
solution.explanation: Raunak = 4 and Shivangi = 6, so Xenia (midway) = 5. Vatsal = 8 and Waseem = 7. Zubair is next to Raunak: seat 3 (seat 5 is taken). Tarak cannot sit next to Zubair, so Tarak = 1 and Urmi = 2. After the interchange Zubair is at seat 8 and Xenia at seat 5, with Shivangi and Waseem between them: two persons.
steps: Raunak 4, Shivangi 6 ⇒ Xenia 5
Vatsal 8, Waseem 7
Zubair 3; Tarak 1, Urmi 2
Interchange: Zubair 8, Vatsal 3
Between 5 and 8: seats 6, 7 ⇒ two
solution.why_others_wrong: One is the count before the interchange; Three and Four count one or both of the end persons.

steps: K 2, O 1
Between 2 and 7: four
solution.why_others_wrong: Three and Five are off by one; Two counts only the boxes between Z and V.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five persons Kanak, Nimesh, Ojasvini, Rudrani and Sushant were born in five different years among 1990, 1994, 2000, 2008 and 2010. Ages are counted in completed years on their birthdays in 2026, so the ages in 2026 are 36, 32, 26, 18 and 16 in some order.
- Kanak is exactly twice as old as Sushant.
- Rudrani is exactly 10 years older than Ojasvini.
- Nimesh is older than Rudrani.

What will be the sum of the ages of Nimesh and Ojasvini on their birthdays in 2030?

solution.concept: Pairs of ages that fit a ratio and a difference
solution.explanation: Ages: 36, 32, 26, 18, 16. 'Twice as old' fits 36 = 2 × 18 or 32 = 2 × 16; '10 years older' fits 36 − 26 or 26 − 16. If Kanak 32 and Sushant 16, the 10-year pair must be Rudrani 36 and Ojasvini 26, leaving Nimesh 18 — younger than Rudrani, which breaks the third clue. So Kanak 36, Sushant 18, Rudrani 26, Ojasvini 16 and Nimesh 32. In 2030 Nimesh will be 36 and Ojasvini 20: 56.
steps: Case Kanak 32: Rudrani 36, Nimesh 18 < Rudrani ✗
Case Kanak 36: Rudrani 26, Ojasvini 16, Nimesh 32 ✓
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 is their sum in 2026; 52 adds four years only once; 60 uses Kanak's age for Nimesh's.

- Aanchal's appointment is 12 days before Jayati's.

solution.concept: Carry dates across a 28-day February
solution.explanation: Aanchal = 23 − 12 = 11 February. Forty-five days later: 17 days take her to 28 February, and 28 more days give 28 March. 1 March 2027 is a Monday (February has exactly four weeks), so 29 March is a Monday and 28 March a Sunday.
steps: Aanchal: 11 February
11 Feb + 17 days = 28 Feb; + 28 days = 28 March
1 Feb Monday ⇒ 1 Mar Monday (28 days)
28 March = 29 March − 1 ⇒ Sunday
solution.why_others_wrong: 29 March treats February as a 29-day month; 27 March and 25 March miscount the days carried over into March.

- Shreyas saved ₹4,800, and Purvi saved ₹1,200 more than Shreyas.
- Mitesh saved ₹2,500 less than Purvi.
- Tilak's savings are exactly midway between Mitesh's and Shreyas's.
- Raghavi saved twice as much as Mitesh.
- Yamika saved less than each of the other five.

By how much do the savings of the second highest saver exceed those of the fourth highest saver?

solution.concept: Fix every value, then rank
solution.explanation: Purvi = 4,800 + 1,200 = 6,000; Mitesh = 6,000 − 2,500 = 3,500; Tilak = (3,500 + 4,800) ÷ 2 = 4,150; Raghavi = 7,000. Order: Raghavi 7,000, Purvi 6,000, Shreyas 4,800, Tilak 4,150, Mitesh 3,500, Yamika. Second (Purvi) − fourth (Tilak) = 1,850.
steps: Purvi 6,000; Mitesh 3,500; Tilak 4,150; Raghavi 7,000
Order: Raghavi > Purvi > Shreyas > Tilak > Mitesh > Yamika
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,200 compares Purvi with Shreyas (third); ₹2,500 compares Purvi with Mitesh (fifth); ₹2,850 compares Raghavi with Tilak.

questions.question_text:
Statement: H ≥ C; C = U; U > B; B ≥ Y; N > H

Conclusions:
I. N > Y
II. H > B

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Reading a combined inequality chain
solution.explanation: Combined: N > H ≥ C = U > B ≥ Y. From N to Y every sign points the same way with strict signs on the path, so N > Y. H ≥ C = U > B gives H > B.
steps: Chain: N > H ≥ C = U > B ≥ Y
I: N > Y, true
II: H > B, true
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: Z < O; O ≤ G; G = D; D > K; K ≥ S

Conclusions:
I. Z < K
II. S < D

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Reading a combined inequality chain
solution.explanation: Combined: Z < O ≤ G = D > K ≥ S. Z and K are on opposite sides of the turn at D, so Z < K is not certain. D > K ≥ S gives S < D.
steps: Chain: Z < O ≤ G = D > K ≥ S
I: reversal at D → no relation
II: D > K ≥ S → S < D, true
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: L ∑ P, P ∂ G, G ∫ F, F ∏ X

Conclusions:
I. L ∂ F
II. X ∂ P

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: L ≥ P > G = F ≤ X. L > F follows (I). X and P lie on opposite sides of the turn at F, so X > P is not certain (II).
steps: Decode: L ≥ P, P > G, G = F, F ≤ X
Chain: L ≥ P > G = F ≤ X
I: L > F, true
II: X > P: reversal at F → not certain
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: B ∇ N, N ∫ T, T ∑ K, K ∂ U

Conclusions:
I. T ∂ U
II. U ∇ N

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: B < N = T ≥ K > U. T ≥ K > U gives T > U (I), and U < K ≤ T = N gives U < N (II).
steps: Decode: B < N, N = T, T ≥ K, K > U
Chain: B < N = T ≥ K > U
I: T > U, true
II: U < N, true
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: E ∏ R, R ∇ H, H ∑ O, O ∫ I

Conclusions:
I. E ∇ I
II. I ∂ R

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: E ≤ R < H ≥ O = I. Both conclusions compare a term left of H with a term right of H, across the turn at H, so neither is certain.
steps: Decode: E ≤ R, R < H, H ≥ O, O = I
Chain: E ≤ R < H ≥ O = I
I: E < I: reversal at H
II: I > R: reversal at H
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: S ∑ A, A ∫ V, V ∑ M, M ∂ Q

Conclusions:
I. S ∂ M
II. S ∫ M

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: S ≥ A = V ≥ M > Q. Only S ≥ M is known, so S > M and S = M are each uncertain, but one of them must be true: either I or II.
steps: Decode: S ≥ A, A = V, V ≥ M, M > Q
S ≥ A = V ≥ M ⇒ S ≥ M
S > M or S = M ⇒ Either I or II
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Either' replaces 'Both' (four-option rule).
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II is true

questions.question_text:

I. G ∂ K
II. K ∑ H

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: G > H ≤ J ≤ K > L. G and K lie on opposite sides of the turn at H, so G > K is not certain. H ≤ J ≤ K gives K ≥ H (II).
steps: Decode: G > H, J ≥ H, J ≤ K, L < K
Chain: G > H ≤ J ≤ K > L
I: reversal at H → not certain
II: K ≥ H, true
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: J ≥ W; W > E; E ≥ Y; P = Y; P ≥ C; D > J

Conclusions:
I. D > C
II. E > C

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Combining six statements into one chain
solution.explanation: Combined: D > J ≥ W > E ≥ Y = P ≥ C. From D to C every sign points the same way and there is a strict sign, so D > C (I). From E to C the signs are only ≥, = and ≥, so E ≥ C — E > C is not certain (II).
steps: Rewrite as one chain: D > J ≥ W > E ≥ Y = P ≥ C
I: strict signs on the path ⇒ D > C, true
II: E ≥ Y = P ≥ C has no strict sign ⇒ only E ≥ C
solution.why_others_wrong: A path made only of ≥ and = never proves a strict '>'.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: K < M ≤ A; A = Z; Z > T ≥ O

Which of the following conclusions is definitely true?

solution.concept: Definitely true = holds in every case the chain allows
solution.explanation: Combined: K < M ≤ A = Z > T ≥ O. K < M ≤ A = Z gives K < Z in every case. M, K and T, O lie on opposite sides of the turn at Z, so M > T, O < M and T < K can each be true or false.
steps: Chain: K < M ≤ A = Z > T ≥ O
K < Z: same direction with a strict sign ⇒ definitely true
M > T, O < M, T < K: compare across the turn at Z ⇒ not determined
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of the other three relations crosses the turn at Z, so it may or may not hold.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: M is the husband of N. N is the only daughter of O. P is the son of O. How is M related to P?

solution.concept: A sister's husband is a brother-in-law
solution.explanation: N and P are both children of O, so N is P's sister. M is N's husband, so M is P's brother-in-law.
steps: N (daughter of O) and P (son of O) are siblings
M = husband of P's sister ⇒ brother-in-law
solution.why_others_wrong: M shares no parent with P; he is in P's generation, so he is neither P's father-in-law nor his uncle.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: Decode left to right and track generations
solution.explanation: K is L's wife. L is M's brother, and M is N's daughter, so L is N's son. K, the wife of N's son, is N's daughter-in-law (whether N is the father or the mother).
steps: K ▽ L: K is L's wife
L △ M and M ○ N: L is a child (son) of N
Wife of one's son ⇒ daughter-in-law
solution.why_others_wrong: Daughter is M's relation to N; K is M's sister-in-law, not N's; Mother puts K a generation too high.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Kamini has exactly two children, one son and one daughter. Neha is Kamini's daughter-in-law, and Ojas is Neha's son. Devendra is Kamini's husband. Riya's mother is Devendra's only daughter, and Prem is the husband of Riya's mother. Each person mentioned has only one spouse. How is Prem related to Ojas?

solution.concept: Identify each spouse first, then the generations
solution.explanation: Neha is Kamini's daughter-in-law, so she is the wife of Kamini's only son; Ojas's father is therefore Kamini's son. Devendra's only daughter is Kamini's daughter (Devendra is Kamini's husband), i.e. the sister of Ojas's father. Prem is her husband, so Prem is the husband of Ojas's paternal aunt: his uncle.
steps: Daughter-in-law of Kamini ⇒ wife of Kamini's only son ⇒ Ojas's father = Kamini's son
Riya's mother = Kamini's daughter = sister of Ojas's father
Prem = her husband ⇒ Ojas's uncle
solution.why_others_wrong: Prem is Riya's father, not Ojas's; he is the brother-in-law of Ojas's father, not of Ojas; he is in the parents' generation, not the grandparents'.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Uncle (husband of his father's sister)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Kavya walks 9 m towards the west. She then turns right and walks 12 m, and then turns right again and walks 4 m. How far is she now from her starting point, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Net displacement
solution.explanation: Right from west is north, and right from north is east. She ends 9 − 4 = 5 m west and 12 m north of the start: √(25 + 144) = 13 m, towards the north-west.
steps: Right = north; 12 m → (−9, 12)
Right = east; 4 m → (−5, 12)
solution.why_others_wrong: North-East forgets that she is still 5 m west; 15 m uses 9 and 12 as the legs; 12 m, North ignores the west part.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Point Q is 7 m east of point P. Point R is 7 m north of point Q. Point S is 3 m west of point R. In which direction is point S with respect to point P?

solution.concept: Place every point on a grid
solution.explanation: Take P at (0, 0). Q = (7, 0), R = (7, 7) and S = (4, 7). S is 4 m east and 7 m north of P: north-east.
steps: S − P = (+4, +7) ⇒ North-East
solution.why_others_wrong: North-West would need S to be west of P; North and East ignore one of the two components.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Soon after sunrise, Mehul stood in an open field with his back to the sun. He then turned 90° anticlockwise. Which direction is he facing now?

solution.concept: The morning sun is in the east
solution.explanation: After sunrise the sun is in the east. With his back to the sun, Mehul faces west. A 90° anticlockwise turn (a left turn) from west gives south.
steps: Morning sun in the east ⇒ back to the sun = facing west
Anticlockwise 90° from west ⇒ south
solution.why_others_wrong: North is a clockwise turn from west; East would mean facing the sun; West ignores the turn.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A boy is facing south-west. He turns 135° anticlockwise and then 270° clockwise. Which direction is he facing now?

solution.concept: Net turn = clockwise − anticlockwise
solution.explanation: Net turn: 270° clockwise − 135° anticlockwise = 135° clockwise. South-west is 225°; 225° + 135° = 360°: north.
steps: Net: 135° clockwise
solution.why_others_wrong: South turns the net amount the wrong way; East stops after the first turn; North-West adds only 90°.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A car travels 20 km towards the north, then turns right and travels 21 km. How far is the car from its starting point, and in which direction?

solution.concept: A 20-21-29 right triangle
solution.explanation: Right from north is east. The car is 21 km east and 20 km north of the start: √(400 + 441) = √841 = 29 km, towards the north-east.
steps: Right = east 21 → (21, 20)
solution.why_others_wrong: 41 km adds the legs; North-West takes the turn as a left turn; 21 km, East ignores the north leg.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Ira and Jai start from the same point. Ira walks 6 km north, turns right and walks 8 km. Jai walks 6 km south, turns left and walks 8 km. How far apart are they now, and in which direction is Ira from Jai?

solution.concept: Put both end points on one grid
solution.explanation: Ira: north 6, then right (east) 8 ⇒ (8, 6). Jai: south 6, then left (from south, left is east) 8 ⇒ (8, −6). Both are 8 km east of the start, so Ira is exactly 12 km north of Jai.
steps: Jai: facing south, left = east ⇒ (8, −6)
Difference (0, 12) ⇒ 12 km, North
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 km, North-East takes Jai's left as west; 12 km, South is Jai's direction from Ira; 20 km adds all the legs.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the straight-line distance between L and M, and in which direction is M from L?

solution.concept: Decode, then use a 6-8-10 triangle
solution.explanation: M is 6 m east and 8 m north of L: √(36 + 64) = 10 m, north-east.
steps: Coordinates (east, north) in metres with L at (0, 0): L (0, 0), K (6, 0), M (6, 8), N (0, 8), O (0, -8), T (-6, -8)
√(6² + 8²) = 10 m, North-East
solution.why_others_wrong: 14 m adds the legs; North-West mistakes α for west; 8 m, North ignores the east part.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How far is point T from point M, and in which direction is T from M?

solution.concept: Difference of two decoded positions
solution.explanation: T = (−6, −8) and M = (6, 8). T is 12 m west and 16 m south of M: √(144 + 256) = 20 m, towards the south-west.
steps: Coordinates (east, north) in metres with L at (0, 0): L (0, 0), K (6, 0), M (6, 8), N (0, 8), O (0, -8), T (-6, -8)
√(12² + 16²) = 20 m, South-West
solution.why_others_wrong: North-East is M's direction from T; 28 m adds the legs; 16 m, South ignores the west part.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which point lies exactly midway between N and O?

solution.concept: Midpoint of two points
solution.explanation: N = (0, 8) and O = (0, −8) lie on one north–south line; their midpoint is (0, 0), which is L.
steps: Coordinates (east, north) in metres with L at (0, 0): L (0, 0), K (6, 0), M (6, 8), N (0, 8), O (0, -8), T (-6, -8)
solution.why_others_wrong: K, M and T are 6 m east or west of that line.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: At about 7 am on a clear day, the shadow of a vertical pole P ends at point Q, 4 m from the foot of the pole. Ravi starts at Q, walks straight to the pole, continues 5 m in the same direction beyond it, then turns left and walks 12 m. How far is Ravi from Q now, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Morning shadows point west
solution.explanation: At 7 am the sun is in the east, so the shadow points west: Q is 4 m west of the pole. Walking from Q to the pole and 5 m beyond means walking east 9 m. A left turn from east is north, 12 m. Ravi is 9 m east and 12 m north of Q: √(81 + 144) = 15 m, north-east.
steps: Morning: sun east ⇒ shadow west ⇒ Q is 4 m west of P
Q → P → 5 m beyond = 9 m east
Left of east = north: 12 m
√(9² + 12²) = 15 m, North-East
solution.why_others_wrong: 13 m measures from the pole instead of from Q; South-East takes the left turn as south; 21 m adds the legs.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A delivery rider starts from the depot and rides 5 km towards the south. She turns left and rides 9 km, turns right and rides 7 km, turns right again and rides 21 km, and finally turns left and rides 4 km. How far is she from the depot, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Track the facing after every turn
solution.explanation: Left from south is east (9 km); right from east is south (7 km); right from south is west (21 km); left from west is south (4 km). Net: east 9 − 21 = 12 km west; south 5 + 7 + 4 = 16 km. √(144 + 256) = 20 km, south-west.
steps: √(12² + 16²) = 20 km, South-West
solution.why_others_wrong: South-East ignores that the 21 km west leg overshoots; 28 km adds the legs; 16 km, South drops the west part.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'flows'?

solution.concept: Remove the codes of the shared words
solution.explanation: In sentence 1, river = ra (shared with sentence 3) and fast = ki (shared with sentence 2), so flows = mo.
steps: river = ra; fast = ki
Leftover in 'mo ki ra' ⇒ flows = mo
solution.why_others_wrong: ki is 'fast', ra is 'river' and te is 'cross'.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which word is coded as 'pu'?

solution.concept: The unshared code of a sentence
solution.explanation: Sentence 2 is 'fast boats sail' = 'ki pu zo'. fast = ki and boats = zo, so pu = sail.
steps: fast = ki (1 & 2); boats = zo (2 & 3)
pu ⇒ sail
solution.why_others_wrong: boats = zo, fast = ki, cross = te.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'cross river'?

solution.concept: Two codes at once
solution.explanation: river = ra (common to sentences 1 and 3). In sentence 3, boats = zo, so cross = te. 'cross river' = 'te ra' (in any order).
steps: river = ra
boats = zo ⇒ cross = te
solution.why_others_wrong: zo is 'boats', mo is 'flows' and ki is 'fast'.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, PENCIL is written as EPCNLI. How is MARKET written in that code?

solution.concept: Letters swapped in pairs
solution.explanation: PENCIL → (PE)(NC)(IL) → EP CN LI: each pair of letters is interchanged. MARKET → (MA)(RK)(ET) → AM KR TE = AMKRTE.
steps: Pairs: PE→EP, NC→CN, IL→LI
MARKET: MA→AM, RK→KR, ET→TE ⇒ AMKRTE
solution.why_others_wrong: TEKRAM reverses the word; AMRKTE does not swap the middle pair; MAKRET swaps only the middle pair.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code language, ROAD is written as WTFI. How is PATH written in that code language?

solution.concept: Every letter moves the same number of places
solution.explanation: R→W, O→T, A→F, D→I: every letter moves 5 places forward. P→U, A→F, T→Y, H→M: UFYM.
steps: PATH +5 ⇒ UFYM
solution.why_others_wrong: UFZM moves T six places; KVOC moves every letter back; UEYM moves A only four places.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, FAN is written as 60 and BOX is written as 40. How is COT written in that code?

solution.concept: Reverse alphabetical positions (A = 26, …, Z = 1)
solution.explanation: Counting from Z = 1 to A = 26: F 21 + A 26 + N 13 = 60; B 25 + O 12 + X 3 = 40. COT: C 24 + O 12 + T 7 = 43.
steps: Reverse positions: F 21, A 26, N 13 ⇒ 60 ✓
solution.why_others_wrong: 38 is the ordinary sum of positions (3 + 15 + 20); 47 and 45 miscount one letter's reverse position.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, BED is written as 254 and HAD as 814. How is FACE written in that code?

solution.concept: Each letter becomes its alphabetical position
steps: Letters → positions: BED 2-5-4, HAD 8-1-4
solution.why_others_wrong: 6153 swaps C and E; 7135 takes F as 7; 6134 takes E as 4.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'OMEN'?

solution.concept: Condition (i): vowel first, consonant last
solution.explanation: O is a vowel and N a consonant, so condition (i) applies: the codes of O (8) and N (5) are interchanged. O M E N → 5 $ 9 8.
steps: Table: O 8, M $, E 9, N 5
Condition (i) ⇒ swap first and last codes ⇒ 5$98
solution.why_others_wrong: 8$95 ignores the condition; $598 swaps the wrong letters; 5$9★ mixes conditions (i) and (iii).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'AROMA'?

solution.concept: Condition (ii): vowels at both ends
solution.explanation: A is a vowel at both ends, so both A's take the code of the second letter, R (&): & & 8 $ &.
steps: Second letter R = &
First and last letters → & ⇒ &&8$&
solution.why_others_wrong: 4&8$4 ignores the condition; 4$8&4 reverses the word; ★&8$★ wrongly applies the ★ rule.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'DUSK'?

solution.concept: No condition applies to consonants at both ends
solution.explanation: D and K are both consonants, so none of the conditions applies: D @, U 6, S 3, K 2 ⇒ @632.
steps: First D, last K: both consonants
Plain table codes ⇒ @632
solution.why_others_wrong: 263@ wrongly applies condition (i); @63★ wrongly applies (iii); #632 uses the code of H for D.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'TUBE'?

solution.concept: Condition (iii): consonant first, vowel last
solution.explanation: T is a consonant and E a vowel, so condition (iii) applies: the last letter is coded as ★. T U B E → © 6 % ★.
steps: Table: T ©, U 6, B %, E 9
Condition (iii) ⇒ last code ★ ⇒ ©6%★
solution.why_others_wrong: ©6%9 ignores the condition; ★6%© puts ★ first and moves ©; 6©%9 rearranges the codes.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'sunlight'?

solution.concept: Strip the shared codes
solution.explanation: plants = su (shared by sentences 2 and 3) and need = ra (shared by sentences 3 and 4), so in 'su ra tu' sunlight = tu.
steps: plants = su; need = ra
sunlight = tu
solution.why_others_wrong: su is 'plants', ra 'need' and vo 'to'.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which word is coded as 'vo'?

solution.concept: Leftover code of a sentence
solution.explanation: Sentence 4 'need to save' = 'ra ka vo'. need = ra and save = ka (shared with sentence 1), so vo = to.
steps: need = ra; save = ka
vo ⇒ to
solution.why_others_wrong: need = ra, save = ka and the = ne.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which word does the code 'lo' stand for?

solution.concept: When two words always appear together
solution.explanation: 'water' and 'daily' occur together in sentences 1 and 2 and nowhere else, so their codes 'lo' and 'mi' cannot be told apart: 'lo' is either 'water' or 'daily'.
steps: water, daily appear only in sentences 1 and 2
Their codes lo, mi cannot be separated
solution.why_others_wrong: Choosing one of the two words assumes information the sentences do not give; 'the' is ne.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, CASTLE is written as TBDFMU. How is BRIDGE written in that code?

solution.concept: Reverse each half, then move every letter one step forward
solution.explanation: CASTLE → halves CAS | TLE → reversed SAC | ELT → each letter +1: TBD | FMU. BRIDGE → BRI | DGE → IRB | EGD → +1: JSC | FHE = JSCFHE.
steps: CAS → SAC → TBD; TLE → ELT → FMU
BRI → IRB → JSC; DGE → EGD → FHE
solution.why_others_wrong: IRBEGD stops before the +1 step; CSJEHF adds 1 without reversing the halves; JSCHFE reverses the second half wrongly.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, 4716 is written as 8396 and 2053 is written as 5724. How is 6481 written in that code?

solution.concept: Add 2 to each digit, then reverse
steps: Reverse → 3068
solution.why_others_wrong: 8603 skips the reversal; 1846 only reverses; 3069 adds 3 to the last digit.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, PLANT is written as OKBMS and CREDIT is written as BQFCJS. How is MOBILE written in that code?

solution.concept: Vowels and consonants move differently
solution.explanation: In PLANT the consonants move one step back (P→O, L→K, N→M, T→S) and the vowel A moves one step forward (A→B); CREDIT confirms it (E→F, I→J). MOBILE: M→L, O→P, B→A, I→J, L→K, E→F = LPAJKF.
steps: Consonants −1, vowels +1
M L, O P, B A, I J, L K, E F
solution.why_others_wrong: NPCJMF moves every letter forward; LNAHKD moves every letter back; LPAJKD moves the final E back instead of forward.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, BANK is written as CCQO and SHIP is written as TJLT. How is WORLD written in that code?

solution.concept: Shift by the letter's place in the word
solution.explanation: Each letter moves forward by its position in the word: B+1 = C, A+2 = C, N+3 = Q, K+4 = O. SHIP: S+1 T, H+2 J, I+3 L, P+4 T. WORLD: W+1 X, O+2 Q, R+3 U, L+4 P, D+5 I = XQUPI.
steps: Shifts +1, +2, +3, +4 (+5 for a 5th letter)
Check BANK → CCQO, SHIP → TJLT
WORLD → XQUPI
solution.why_others_wrong: XQUPH moves the 5th letter by 4; XPSMH moves every letter by 1; YQUPI moves the first letter by 2.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code language, each word is coded by a rule, and the codes are written in the same order as the words. 'safe money transfer' is written as 'T4 N5 U8', and 'quick loan' is written as 'R5 M4'. How is 'fast online payment' written in that code language?

solution.concept: Code = letter after the first letter + number of letters
solution.explanation: safe → S+1 = T and 4 letters: T4; money → N5; transfer → U8; quick → R5; loan → M4. fast → G4, online → P6, payment → Q7.
steps: Letter part: the letter after the word's first letter
Number part: length of the word
fast G4, online P6, payment Q7
solution.why_others_wrong: F4 O6 P7 does not shift the first letter; G4 P6 Q8 miscounts 'payment' (7 letters); G4 P5 Q7 miscounts 'online' (6 letters).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

Q 7 % D E 3 & 8 K # U 1 J @ 5 X Z 6 $ A

Which element is 4th to the left of the 6th element from the right end?

solution.concept: Convert a right-end position, then move left

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: The tank now holds 1,200 ÷ 4 = 300 litres and needs 900 more; at 50 litres a minute that takes 18 minutes (I). After 5 minutes it holds 300 + 250 = 550 litres, less than half (600), so II is false.

After 5 min: 550 L < 600 L ⇒ II false

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: The city's ban on plastic bags in shops has reduced the amount of plastic waste the city produces, because the number of plastic bags reaching the city landfill fell by 40% in the six months after the ban.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Many shopkeepers supported the ban when it was announced
Cloth bags cost more than plastic bags
The ban was widely reported in the city's newspapers
During the same six months, a new recycling unit began collecting most plastic waste directly from homes, so much less plastic of every kind reached the landfill

solution.concept: Weaken: the measured fall may come from a change in where waste goes, not from less waste
solution.explanation: The evidence is the count of bags at the landfill. If a new unit diverted plastic away from the landfill, the count would fall even if the city produced as much plastic waste as before, so the evidence no longer supports the conclusion.
steps: Evidence: fewer bags at the landfill
Conclusion: less plastic waste produced
Weakener: plastic diverted to recycling ⇒ landfill count no longer measures waste produced
solution.why_others_wrong: Shopkeepers' support, the price of cloth bags and press coverage say nothing about how much plastic waste the city produces.
solution.final_answer: Option D: During the same six months, a new recycling unit began collecting most plastic waste directly from homes, so much less plastic of every kind reached the landfill
